title: Ali's words
hookLine: sermons and sayings attributed to Ali, gathered in Nahj al-Balagha, are especially treasured by Shia Muslims

cards: A governor is about to leave for his new province, and a letter is put in his hands. It tells him how to treat the people he'll rule, and somewhere in it is a line worth stopping on: people are of two kinds.
Either your brother in faith, or your equal in creation. The letter is attributed to Ali, written to Malik al-Ashtar as he went to govern Egypt. It's one of many pieces gathered in a single book.

teach.h: NAHJ AL-BALAGHA: THE PATH OF ELOQUENCE.
teach.b: The book is called Nahj al-Balagha, the path of eloquence. Its compiler gathered sermons, letters and short sayings attributed to Ali, arranged in those three parts.
Shia Muslims treasure it especially, reading it alongside the Qur'an and the hadith as words from their first Imam.

Sunni readers have also prized it, often for the beauty of its Arabic, and some scholars question whether every piece in it goes back to Ali himself. So this path says attributed, and means it. Now, the words.

teach.h: A BROTHER IN FAITH, OR AN EQUAL IN CREATION.
teach.b: Either your brother in faith, or your equal in creation. It leaves nobody out. If someone shares your religion, they're your brother or sister.
If they don't, they still came from the same Maker as you, and they're owed the same justice. For a ruler about to hold power over many kinds of people, that's a job description.

teach.h: WORTH IS WHAT YOU DO WELL.
teach.b: A short saying is about worth: the value of each person lies in what they do well. The saying doesn't name family or wealth. Only what they do well.
And a long letter of advice to his son al-Hasan includes this, in paraphrase: make yourself the measure between you and others.
Want for them what you want for yourself, and dislike for them what you dislike for yourself. Don't be anyone's slave when God made you free. All three are short enough to carry.
This is where the first circle closes: Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman and Ali, four men around the Prophet, each remembered in his own way.

how: Shia Muslims read Nahj al-Balagha for guidance, study it in seminaries and quote it in sermons; Sunni readers also study it, especially for its Arabic style.

games.q: you're a new governor reading your letter of instructions. the people you'll rule follow many faiths. how does the letter ask you to see them?
o: your own faith first, the rest after.
either your brother in faith, or your equal in creation.
by how loyal they are to you.
games.why: the letter attributed to Ali names two kinds of people and leaves nobody out.

practice: Choose one of the three sayings: a brother in faith, or an equal in creation; worth is what you do well; make yourself the measure.
Say it slowly in your head, then bring to mind one person you'll meet today and hold the saying up to them. What would it change about how you treat them?
